item.title: The Bell Experiment, Monadically
item.description: arXiv:2611.26777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bell's theorem says that no classical model satisfying certain independence assumptions can reproduce the correlations that quantum mechanics predicts and experiments observe. In this paper we write the two-party Bell experiment as a small Haskell program, and find those assumptions in its structure: in what each part of the program can see, and in how the parts are composed. The boxes of the two parties compute in one monad, and the experiment that schedules and repeats their trials computes in another; a \emph{membrane} runs the first inside the second. A run keeps the record of its trials, and both of its verdicts, the CHSH value and whether the boxes signal, are read off one table: the empirical model of that run. In this setting, a model is classical when it has three properties. It is \emph{blind}: the hidden strategy of the boxes is drawn without seeing the measurement settings. It is \emph{local}: given that strategy, neither box's outcome depends on the other party's setting. It is \emph{factored}: given the strategy and the settings, the two outcomes are independent. Together, they give the classical bound of $2$. We give them up one at a time and run what results. Without blindness, we get experimental loopholes and superdeterminism. Without factoring, we get quantum boxes, which reach $2\sqrt2$, and the hypothetical PR boxes, which reach $4$, both without signaling. Without locality, we get boxes that rewrite a shared hidden state; whether they signal depends on how that state is sampled. We also compare two ways to check no-signaling: reading it off the run's own table, and estimating it in separate experiments at fixed settings.
item.dc:creator: Chenchao Ding, Amr Sabry

item.title: Compositional Temporal Specifications for Interaction Trees
item.description: arXiv:2611.27553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The correctness of modern effectful programs depends not only on their final results but also on the temporal evolution of observable interactions with their environments. Interaction Trees (ITrees) provide a reusable denotational semantics for such programs by representing effectful computations as potentially infinite trees of observable interactions. However, reusable temporal reasoning over ITrees remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a compositional temporal specification framework for ITrees. We introduce iBuchi, a shallowly embedded temporal specification language based on Choice Trees, which represents finite and infinite interaction traces and supports expressive temporal operators, including sequencing, branching, conjunction, repetition, and Linear Temporal Logic modalities. We define trace- and tree-level satisfaction relations between iBuchi specifications and ITrees, together with compositional reasoning principles for modular verification of effectful programs. We integrate iBuchi into the Dijkstra Monads Forever framework, thereby enabling temporal specifications to compose with conventional Hoare-style specifications and supporting a generator-based encoding of future conditions. We have formally developed and verified our framework in Rocq and demonstrated its expressiveness and compositionality through several non-trivial case studies.
item.dc:creator: Linyu Yang, Jianwei Yin, Mingshuai Chen

item.title: Exposing Call-Shared Stacks to a Meta-Tracing JIT Compiler
item.description: arXiv:2609.23759v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Meta-tracing JIT compilers such as RPython's can optimize accesses to interpreter state when the state is represented in a form that the optimizer can track, such as fixed fields in virtualizable interpreter frames. However, interpreters for stack-based languages such as Forth and Factor use a shared data stack whose depth and per-call usage are not necessarily known statically. Keeping this stack in a heap array may leave memory accesses in compiled traces, while exposing the entire array to the optimizer makes the amount of exposed state depend on its allocated capacity. Conventional stack caching avoids some memory accesses but does not necessarily make cached values visible to a meta-tracing JIT compiler. We propose the stack fragment layout, which divides a shared data stack into a fixed-width top fragment and a shared spill array. The top fragment stores stack values in interpreter fields that a meta-tracing JIT compiler can optimize within traces, while the spill retains deeper values in memory. This representation bounds the amount of JIT-visible stack state independently of the total stack depth, without requiring static stack-effect information. We provide proof sketches showing that the layout preserves the modeled stack operations and, under stated assumptions, that the amount of stack state reconstructed at trace exits is bounded by the fragment width plus constant control state. We implement the layout in RPyForth, an RPython-based Forth interpreter, and RPyFactor, an interpreter for a subset of Factor. Controlled experiments isolate the benefit of exposing the top fragment to the meta-tracing JIT compiler from that of stack caching alone. Across three benchmark suites on two x86-64 machines, this optimization yields suite-level geometric-mean speedups of 1.44-2.11 in RPyForth and 1.42-1.56x in RPyFactor.
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Izawa, Kota Hakamada

item.title: Multi-language Program Logics (Extended Version)
item.description: arXiv:2609.32877v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-world programs are rarely written in a single language: For example, C programs call assembly routines, and high-level languages like OCaml link with low-level C libraries. Yet program logics---one of the most successful techniques for modular program verification---almost exclusively target single-language programs. We present Hotpot, the first framework for building multi-language program logics. Hotpot enables compilation-independent, cross-language reasoning about languages with heterogeneous views of shared state. Hotpot rests on four key ideas: abstract calls to specify calls to unknown functions, lanes and the switching modality to move between languages inside the program logic, uniform integration of refinement reasoning via lanes, and exchanges to translate between separation logic assertions of different languages. We demonstrate that Hotpot allows reusing specifications across implementations in different languages, supports reasoning about higher-order cross-language function calls, and integrates with verified compilation. Hotpot is built on top of Iris and DimSum and mechanized in the Rocq Prover.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Loitzl, Niklas M\"uck, Michael Sammler
